projects.name: Decentralized Document Notary
projects.shortDesc: Blockchain-based document notarization app (Solidity, React, Node.js, Supabase, Cloudflare R2) — deployed on Sepolia, Render & Vercel.
projects.longDesc: The problem: proving a document existed in a specific state at a specific time, without trusting a single company's database to not quietly change it later. Traditional notarization solves this with a person and a stamp; this project solves it by hashing the document client-side and writing that hash to a smart contract on Sepolia — so the proof of existence lives on a public, append-only ledger instead of in someone's private table.
projects.extra: The interesting engineering problem wasn't the smart contract itself (that part is genuinely simple) — it was everything around it. Files themselves are too large and too sensitive to put on-chain, so the actual documents live in Cloudflare R2, with Supabase handling user accounts, metadata, and the mapping between a file and its on-chain hash. The contract only ever sees a hash, never the document. Deployed across three different platforms doing three different jobs — Vercel for the frontend, Render for a small backend service, Sepolia for the actual notarization — which turned out to be a good, if accidental, lesson in keeping deploy responsibilities cleanly separated.

caseStudy.problem: Proving a document existed in a specific, unaltered state at a specific time — without trusting a single company's database not to quietly change that record later. A timestamp in a normal database is only as trustworthy as whoever controls that database.
caseStudy.architecture: The document itself never touches the blockchain. The app hashes the document client-side and writes only that hash to a smart contract on Sepolia. The actual file lives in Cloudflare R2; Supabase manages user accounts and the mapping between a user, a file, and its on-chain hash. The chain's only job is answering one question: did a hash matching this exact document exist at this block?
technicalDecisions: Splitting the system across three platforms deliberately — Vercel for the frontend, Render for backend services, Sepolia for the actual notarization logic — kept 'serve the UI,' 'handle app logic,' and 'provide immutability' as separate concerns, easier to reason about and swap out independently.
Hashing client-side rather than uploading the raw file to any notarization service, so the document's contents never need to be trusted to a third party at all, on-chain or off.
caseStudy.challenges: The interesting engineering problem wasn't the smart contract itself — verifying a hash match is genuinely simple Solidity. The real work was everything around it: keeping the actual file, the hash, and the on-chain record correctly linked across three different platforms without any single point where the record could be quietly altered.
caseStudy.whatILearned: A public blockchain isn't free — gas costs money (even fake testnet money has real friction) and a public chain means the hash is technically visible to anyone, even though the document isn't. For most use cases a signed database record with an audit log is genuinely fine. This project exists for the narrower slice of cases where that isn't good enough, and building it was a good way to actually feel that trade-off rather than just read about it.

projects.name: On-Chain Voting dApp
projects.shortDesc: Solidity (Hardhat) voting contract with a React + ethers.js frontend styled like an official paper ballot.
projects.longDesc: A minimal voting contract, deliberately kept small so the interesting part could be the frontend: a ballot UI styled to look like an actual official paper ballot rather than a typical crypto dashboard. The goal was to test whether a blockchain voting interface could feel familiar to someone who's never touched a wallet before — same visual language as a polling booth, with the wallet connection and transaction confirmation handled quietly in the background.
projects.extra: Hardhat handled local contract testing and deployment scripting; ethers.js bridged the contract calls to the UI. It's a small project, but it's the direct descendant of my final-year university project — same core idea (votes as immutable on-chain records), much cleaner execution.

caseStudy.problem: Most blockchain voting demos look and feel like crypto dashboards, which is exactly wrong for something meant to feel trustworthy to someone who's never touched a wallet. The goal was a ballot that felt like an actual official paper ballot, with the blockchain machinery handled quietly in the background.
caseStudy.architecture: A minimal Solidity voting contract, deliberately kept small so the interesting part could be the frontend. Hardhat handles local contract testing and deployment scripting; ethers.js bridges the contract calls to a React UI styled to look like an official paper ballot rather than a typical Web3 dashboard.
technicalDecisions: Keeping the contract itself minimal on purpose — the design goal was UX and trust, not contract complexity.
Using Hardhat for the local testing/deployment loop, ethers.js for the frontend bridge, and React for a UI intentionally styled away from typical crypto-app visual language.
caseStudy.challenges: Making a wallet-connected, on-chain transaction feel as unremarkable as clicking a checkbox on a government form — hiding the genuinely awkward parts of Web3 UX (wallet connection, transaction confirmation) behind an interface that doesn't ask the user to think about any of it.
caseStudy.whatILearned: This project is the direct descendant of my university final-year project — same core idea, votes as immutable on-chain records — with a much cleaner execution once I wasn't also learning Solidity for the first time while building it.

projects.name: Groq Chat App
projects.shortDesc: Full-stack chat app — Node.js/Express backend calling the Groq API, React (Vite) frontend.
projects.longDesc: A full-stack chat interface built to get hands-on with fast LLM inference — Groq's API serves responses fast enough that the usual 'typing indicator' UX patterns barely matter. The Express backend handles the API calls and keeps the key server-side; the Vite/React frontend is deliberately simple, just a textbox and a response stream, so the focus stays on the model interaction rather than UI chrome.
projects.extra: This project doubled as a testbed for prompt engineering technique — testing how system prompts, temperature, and message history structure change response quality in a low-latency setting.

caseStudy.problem: Getting genuinely hands-on with fast LLM inference, and using a real chat interface as a testbed for prompt engineering technique rather than just reading about it.
caseStudy.architecture: A Node.js/Express backend calls the Groq API and keeps the API key server-side; a React (Vite) frontend handles the chat interface. Groq's low latency is fast enough that the usual 'typing indicator, then a wall of text appears' UX pattern barely matters.
technicalDecisions: Keeping the API key strictly server-side in the Express backend rather than calling Groq directly from the frontend.
Using the app as a deliberate testbed for testing how system prompts, temperature, and message history structure change response quality in a low-latency setting.
caseStudy.challenges: The real lesson wasn't about the UI — it was that prompt engineering is closer to ordinary software engineering than the phrase suggests: the biggest quality gains came from being explicit about output format, scope, and failure modes, not from clever wording.
caseStudy.whatILearned: Temperature and message-history length are load-bearing settings that get less attention than the prompt text itself, but matter just as much for response quality and cost.

projects.name: Election System Using Blockchain (SISC)
projects.shortDesc: Final-year project — permissioned blockchain voting system on Hyperledger Fabric via IBM Blockchain VS Code extension.
projects.longDesc: My university final-year project, and the one that got me into blockchain in the first place. Unlike public, permissionless blockchains, this uses Hyperledger Fabric — a permissioned blockchain, meaning only known, vetted participants can validate transactions. That's a deliberate choice: for something like an election, you often want accountability and known identities behind each validating node, not full anonymity.
projects.extra: Built and deployed through the IBM Blockchain VS Code extension, which handles a lot of the Fabric network scaffolding that would otherwise be painful to configure by hand.
